What Is Per Unit System Impedance and How to Calculate It

What is per unit system impedance? It is the actual impedance in ohms divided by the base impedance of the zone where it sits. Once base MVA and base kV are fixed, every other base follows, and the per unit impedance of a transformer comes out the same whether it is viewed from the HV or LV side.

Per Unit Formula Quick Reference

QuantityFormula
Base current (A)Ibase = MVAbase × 1000 / (√3 × kVbase)
Base impedance (Ω)Zbase = kVbase² / MVAbase
Per unit impedanceZpu = Zactual / Zbase
From percent impedanceZpu = %Z / 100
Change of baseZnew = Zold × (MVAnew / MVAold) × (kVold / kVnew)²
Three phase fault currentIf (pu) = 1 / Zpu, then If (A) = If (pu) × Ibase

Worked Example: Ohms to Per Unit

  1. Choose a 100 MVA base and an 11 kV base for the zone.
  2. Base impedance: Zbase = 11² / 100 = 1.21 Ω.
  3. An 11 kV cable of 0.5 Ω per phase gives Zpu = 0.5 / 1.21 = 0.413 pu.
  4. Base current: Ibase = 100 × 1000 / (1.732 × 11) = 5249 A.
  5. For a bolted fault fed only through this cable from an infinite 1 pu source, If = 1 / 0.413 = 2.42 pu, or about 12.7 kA.

Always convert every impedance to the common base before adding series elements together.
